title: Bob Dylan’s Last-Minute Guitarist Swap: A Chicago Bluesman Saves the Show
summary:
Bob Dylan's June 29 show at the Moody Amphitheater in Austin was supposed to be a routine stop on his tour. But after guitarist Doug Lancio left two weeks prior, replacement Julian Lage had a prior commitment in Brooklyn, and second guitarist Bob Britt abruptly quit with a "Sayonara Bobby" Facebook post, the band was in crisis. Fans speculated wildly: Would a past member return? Would Dylan play as a trio?

The answer came when the lights dimmed and Chicago-based blues guitarist Joel Paterson walked onstage — alone, handling all guitar parts by himself. Paterson is hardly a household name, but he has a long history on the Chicago blues scene, having recorded with Dave "Honey Boy" Edwards, Wanda Jackson, and others. Until this week, he played every Monday with his jazz quartet at the historic Green Mill Cocktail Lounge, which seats about 150 people. He last performed there on June 27, two days before his Dylan debut.

According to early fan reports, Paterson did a stellar job, playing 16 songs including "All Along the Watchtower." It's unclear how much time he had to prepare. He had previously played pedal steel on four Dylan songs for a 2022 Cactus Blossoms EP, which may have helped.

Britt later clarified on Facebook that he left voluntarily for private reasons. Julian Lage's wife confirmed that Lage plans to return for additional dates when his schedule permits. However, Lage couldn't make Austin because he was booked for a Q&A at National Sawdust in Brooklyn. Dylan's tour continues, with the U.S. leg ending Aug. 1 in Nashville. Paterson's role remains uncertain — he could be a temporary fill-in or a permanent member. The Never Ending Tour hasn't seen this much drama in a long time.
why_it_matters: This last-minute substitution shows how even legendary artists must adapt when plans fall apart, and it highlights the network of skilled musicians working quietly in local scenes — like Joel Paterson at a 150-seat jazz club — who can step into the biggest stages. For younger listeners, it’s a reminder that the music world is interconnected and that talent often exists unseen until a sudden opportunity reveals it.

background_read: Bob Dylan’s current touring band has undergone many changes over the years — his so-called 'Never Ending Tour' began in 1988 and has featured dozens of musicians. It’s not uncommon for guitarists to leave mid-tour due to personal reasons or other commitments.

Joel Paterson, the emergency replacement, is deeply rooted in the Chicago blues tradition, playing the same circuit that launched legends like Muddy Waters and Buddy Guy. His regular Monday gig at the Green Mill Cocktail Lounge (a Chicago jazz club founded in 1907, once a hangout for Al Capone) usually draws just 150 people — a stark contrast to Dylan’s amphitheater crowds.

Dylan’s Austin show took place at the Moody Amphitheater, an outdoor venue in Waterloo Park that opened in 2021 and seats over 5,000. The concert was part of a U.S. leg that wraps up in Nashville on August 1.

Julian Lage, the guitarist who missed the Austin gig, is a prominent jazz guitarist who also plays with Dylan — his 'prior commitment' was a Q&A at National Sawdust, a Brooklyn arts venue founded in 2015 that champions experimental music.

The abrupt departure of Bob Britt — who had been with Dylan’s band since 2019 — and the online speculation show how social media can amplify backstage drama, turning routine musician changes into public mysteries.

perspectives.perspective: Positive (Dylan’s team and fans at the show)
perspectives.description: The quick fix with Paterson saved the concert — early reports praised his performance, and the audience witnessed a unique moment in Dylan’s long history. It also gave a deserving but under-the-radar Chicago bluesman a chance to shine on a major platform, potentially launching his career to a wider audience.

Bob Britt’s abrupt Facebook post and the public speculation felt unprofessional and disrespectful to the tour. Some fans might feel the show was compromised, missing the planned dual-guitar sound they expected, and the drama overshadowed the music. The uncertainty about Paterson’s status adds confusion rather than excitement.

Dylan’s touring band has always been a revolving door — this is part of the Never Ending Tour’s DNA as a constant work in progress. The incident mirrors past crises like the 2002 guitarist change before a Japan tour. Such shake-ups often renew the sound, keeping the setlists fresh and the performances unpredictable.

The remainder of the tour will test whether Paterson can maintain the quality shown in Austin, and if Lage’s return blends smoothly. If Paterson fits well, he could become a permanent member and influence future recordings. The situation also raises questions about how much time artists should give for replacements — a single day’s notice might not be sustainable.
